extracted.intended_audience: researchers, research-integrity professionals, journalists, and readers interested in scientific publishing and retractions
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and de facto standards used to decide when to issue expressions of concern, corrections (errata), authorship notices, or full retractions for a scientific paper — including roles of institutional investigations, availability of raw data, and journal/COPE guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expression of Concern when data may not be representative
rubrics_metrics.description: The journal had previously "issued an Editorial Expression of Concern... noting the data presented in the paper may not be 'fully representative' of the experiments."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An expression of concern is used to flag potentially unreliable or suspect data while investigations proceed; it signals that published results might not be fully representative or trustworthy pending further review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retraction following institutional request or investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: A journal can retract a paper "upon request from the Karolinska Institutet (KI)" after an institutional investigation concluded some authors were guilty of scientific misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional findings of misconduct or significant technical problems can prompt journals to retract articles, either at the institution's request or after the journal's own assessment. Retraction notices should state the basis (e.g., technical issues raised by an investigation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigation findings (technical issues and misconduct) as grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: The retraction referenced a report "prepared by the Expert Group for Misconduct in Research" and cited "technical issues raised by this investigation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independent or institutional investigations that identify technical flaws, procedural errors, or misconduct provide primary evidence used by journals to justify editorial actions such as expressions of concern, corrections, or retractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Loss/unavailability of original/raw data undermines verifiability
rubrics_metrics.description: Macchiarini stated that "Karolinska Institutet lost some of the animal house records... including some of the original data logs concerning this experiment," and that he "cannot prove all the raw data beyond the doubt of those who mistrust and accuse us."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Missing or lost primary data (notebooks, original logs) prevents independent verification and can be treated as sufficient cause for retraction if results cannot be substantiated. Preservation and ability to produce raw data are critical to defend published findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: COPE guidelines inform but do not mechanically demand retraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Macchiarini: "I do stand by the findings of the manuscript, and in that respect I believe the [Committee on Publication Ethics] guidelines do not demand retraction from my point of view."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: COPE provides guidance on when to correct or retract papers, but application requires judgment. Not all errors mandate retraction under COPE; editors must consider severity, intent, verifiability, and whether correction suffices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Erratum/correction appropriate for fixable methodological/phrasing/statistical issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Macchiarini argued that "both the Journal and the authors would have been satisfied with the outcome of an erratum" to "correct our phrasing regarding the weights and the statistical analysis and improve the methodological description of the CT scan."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When problems are limited to wording, statistical reporting, or method descriptions that do not undermine the integrity of the data or indicate misconduct, issuing an erratum or corrigendum is often the appropriate remedy rather than retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors' agreement and authorship contactability noted in notices
rubrics_metrics.description: The retraction notice lists authors who "agree with this retraction" and those who "could not be reached for comment."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retraction notices commonly state which authors agreed or disagreed and note unreachable authors. Journals document author consent/status for transparency; lack of response does not necessarily block editorial action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial notices to remove or correct authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: The article notes that a journal "has also issued multiple notices to remove four authors."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals may issue editorial notices to correct authorship (add/remove authors) when investigations find authorship improprieties or errors. Authorship corrections are part of editorial remedies distinct from retraction/correction of content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of reputational and field-wide trust implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Macchiarini emphasizes that media coverage implying fabrication "is important for the entire field of tissue engineering (peers must be able to have faith in what is published in reputable journals...), and also most especially for the students and early career researchers whose work this manuscript represents."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and institutions weigh the broader impact on community trust, early-career researchers, and the field's reputation when deciding whether to correct, retract, or publicly investigate work; preserving confidence in the literature is a stated objective of such actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation/usage context may be recorded but is not by itself a corrective criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: The piece notes the retracted article "has been cited nine times, according to Clarivate Analytics’ Web of Science."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While citation counts and continued use of a paper may factor into the urgency of corrective action, citation alone does not determine whether an erratum or retraction is warranted; the core issue remains the reliability and verifiability of the underlying data and integrity of the work.
